title: Dreams in prison (Genesis 40)
hookLine: the butler and the baker; the butler forgets him

lines: TWO SAD FACES IN THE MORNING.
cards: I'll put in a word for you. I'll send your résumé along. I won't forget this.
Everyone has had a friend who promised, and then, nothing. Not cruelty. They just got busy with their own good news.
In Joseph's prison, two new men arrive from Pharaoh's own household: the chief butler, who pours Pharaoh's wine, and the chief baker. Both have fallen out of favor.
One morning Joseph, who is looking after them, notices that they both look miserable.

teach.b: Start with what Joseph does first. He notices. A prisoner himself, falsely accused, he still looks at the faces around him and asks, why do you look so sad today?
We each had a dream, they say, and there's nobody to interpret it.

teach.h: DO NOT INTERPRETATIONS BELONG TO GOD?
teach.b: Joseph answers: "Do not interpretations belong to God?" Tell me. The butler dreams of a vine with three branches; the grapes ripen, and he squeezes them into Pharaoh's cup.

teach.h: THREE DAYS: ONE RESTORED, ONE HANGED.
teach.b: Joseph says: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head and give you your job back. Then he asks for one thing. Remember me when it goes well for you.

Mention me to Pharaoh. I was stolen from my land, and here too I've done nothing to deserve this dungeon. The baker, encouraged, tells his dream: three baskets of bread on his head, and birds eating from the top one.
Joseph's answer is grim: in three days Pharaoh will lift up your head too, but off of you. Three days later, on Pharaoh's birthday, it all happens exactly as Joseph said.
Then the chapter ends with one of the loneliest verses in the Torah: "Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgot him."
It says it twice, remember and forget, as if to let it sink in. Two more full years go by. A midrash reads those two years as a lesson for Joseph himself, about putting too much hope in a man.
But you can read the verse the other way too: as a lesson for the butler, and for anyone who ever got out and left someone behind.

how: Jewish tradition calls gratitude hakarat ha-tov, recognizing the good, and teaches that forgetting a kindness done to you is a real failing; the butler is the classic example.

o: a riddle the guards asked Joseph to solve
visions sent to free Joseph from prison
two dreams read, then Joseph forgotten

games.q: who dreamed what — tap the pairs.
p: why do you look so sad today?

s: Joseph took credit for reading the dreams
he said: "Do not interpretations belong to God?"
both dreams came true exactly as Joseph said
on the third day, Pharaoh's birthday, the butler was restored and the baker hanged.
the butler told Pharaoh about Joseph right away
"Yet did not the chief butler remember Joseph, but forgot him." two more years passed.

games.q: you're Joseph. you've just told the butler he'll get his job back in three days. what do you ask him for?
o: to remember you and mention you to Pharaoh.
games.why: he asks to be remembered. and the butler forgets him, for two full years.

practice: Think back to a hard stretch in your life and someone who helped you through it: a teacher, a neighbor, a friend who gave you a couch, or a reference, or just time.
Picture their face, remember exactly what they did, and ask yourself whether they know it mattered.

wordCard.voice: Dreams in prison. Joseph reads the dreams of the butler and the baker, asks to be remembered, and is forgotten for two more years.

orig.note: Hebrew: to remember. the chapter ends with this word and its opposite, shakhach, to forget.

carryVoice: Your line: don't forget Joseph. The butler did, for two whole years. See you at Pharaoh's court tomorrow.
